snip.t: Fat embolism syndrome is a rapidly progressive, potentially fatal complication involving pain, respiratory distress, changes in mental status, and multiorgan system failure.

Pancreatitis, fat embolism, and sepsis are classic INDIRECT causes (via systemic inflammatory mediators reaching the lung through the bloodstream); inhalational injury is also direct, but aspiration is the most commonly cited direct cause in this context.*
Chest findings (crepitations, tachypnoea): Acute chest syndrome – pulmonary vaso‑occlusion, infection, or fat embolism.
could also occur as a result of fat embolism originating from the distal bone in VOC
Common triggers: sepsis, aspiration, pancreatitis, trauma, fat embolism
Fracture of long bones (e.g., femur) releases marrow fat into the circulation, the classic cause of fat embolism syndrome.

qs.q: Fat embolism syndrome typically develops within what time frame after long bone fracture?
o: More than 4 weeks after the initial trauma
qs.e: Fat embolism syndrome (petechiae, neurologic symptoms, respiratory failure) typically develops 24–72 hours after massive trauma or long bone fracture. The mechanism involves mechanical obstruction plus toxic fatty acid release causing endothelial damage.
